readerTitle: Two businesses: one sells, the other gets bought
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (만두 가게, 프로젝트 관리 앱) + 가상 적용 (기장 대행) · 개념 정의는 Marc Andreessen(2007) 에세이 인용
insight: 제품-시장 적합성은 제품의 품질이 아니라 특정 고객 집단과의 맞물림이며, 내가 수요를 미는지 수요가 나를 끄는지로 느낄 수 있다.
misconception: 매출이 크거나 제품이 잘 만들어졌으면 제품-시장 적합성이 있는 것이다.

sources.text: Andreessen, M. (2007, June 25). The Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4: The only thing that matters. pmarchive.com
만두 가게, 앱, 기장 대행 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Andreessen 정의 인용문 "being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market"의 원문 표현과 2007년 게시일을 게시 전 원문에서 다시 확인하세요.
4번 카드의 "the market pulls the product out of the company"는 Andreessen 에세이 내용(좋은 시장에서는 시장이 스타트업에서 제품을 끌어낸다)을 의역한 것입니다. 직접 인용 부호를 쓰지 않았는지 확인하세요.
용어의 최초 사용자는 Andy Rachleff로 알려져 있으나 카드에는 "popularized"로만 적어 최초 사용자 주장을 피했습니다.
만두 가게 월 $12,000, 앱 월 $40,000 등 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치이며 계산이 필요한 내용은 없습니다.

cards.title: Two businesses: one sells, the other gets bought
body: A dumpling counter earns $12,000 a month. A project-planning app earns $40,000.
On paper, the app is winning. But spend one week with each founder, and you'll notice something the revenue doesn't show.

image.label: A busy dumpling counter beside a laptop showing an ad dashboard
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 점심시간 줄이 길게 선 작은 만두 가게, 오른쪽은 광고 대시보드를 띄운 노트북 앞에서 지친 창업자. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which one is closer to product-market fit?
body: **Dumpling counter, $12,000/month:** no ads. A line forms at noon and it sells out by 1:30 most days. Regulars bring coworkers.
**Project app, $40,000/month:** most new users arrive through paid ads and launch discounts. Many cancel within a few months, so the team keeps refilling the bucket.

options.text: The app. $40,000 a month proves people want it
options.feedback: Revenue shows people paid once. It doesn't show whether they'd come without the ads and discounts, or stay after.

options.text: The dumpling counter. Customers come without being pushed
options.feedback: Smaller, but demand is running ahead of supply. That pull is what this lesson is about.

options.text: Impossible to say. They're too different in size
options.feedback: Fair caution, since you'd want more data. But size isn't the question here. How customers arrive and whether they return tells you a lot.

cards.title: Different businesses, different problems.
body: Look at what keeps each founder up at night.
list: **Dumpling founder:** how to make dough faster, add a second steamer and shorten the line
**App founder:** which ad to test next, how big a discount to offer, why last month's users left
cards.callout: One founder pushes demand. The other is pulled along by it.
cards.softwareNote: In software, push often looks like rising ad spend per signup and a sales team chasing every deal. Pull looks like users inviting colleagues and complaining loudly when the product goes down.

cards.title: Product-market fit
body: **Product-market fit** means a specific group of customers wants what you offer so much that demand starts pulling your business forward.

Investor Marc Andreessen popularized the term in a 2007 essay. He defined it as "being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market." His point: when you have it, the market pulls the product out of the company. When you don't, no amount of pushing makes up for it.

image.label: A cart pushed uphill versus a cart pulled by a crowd
image.brief: 두 장면 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 한 사람이 혼자 수레를 언덕 위로 미는 모습 "Push". 오른쪽: 사람들이 줄을 잡고 수레를 끌어당기는 모습 "Pull". 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Fit belongs to the match, not the product.
body: Imagine the same dumplings, same recipe, same price, in an office park that empties at 5 p.m. and has a canteen already. The food hasn't changed. The fit has.
The app may be well built too. Its problem might not be quality at all. It may be serving people who don't feel the problem strongly enough to stay.
That's why fit has two halves: **a product** and **a group of customers** who badly want it.

cards.title: Fit comes in degrees, and it can fade.
body: Fit isn't a switch that flips once. Early on, you may have strong pull from a few customers and none from the rest.
It can also slip. If the offices near the dumpling counter move to remote work, the noon line shrinks. The dumplings are just as good. The market around them changed.
So treat fit as something you keep checking, not a badge you earn once.

cards.title: Fit is not the finish line.
body: Fit doesn't guarantee profit. The dumpling counter can sell out daily and still lose money if rent eats every dollar.
It also doesn't promise size. You can have strong pull in a market too small to grow in.
And "pull" is a feeling at first. Founders who want fit badly tend to see it everywhere. Later lessons in this unit show how to check it with behavior, not hope.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping service.
body: You run a bookkeeping service for small businesses. Looking back at the last three months, which one suggests fit is forming?

options.text: Month 1: a record 30 new clients, after a 30% discount and a paid ad campaign
options.feedback: Big numbers, but you pushed hard to get them. You don't yet know who would have come, or stayed, at full price.

options.text: Month 2: only 8 new clients, but 6 were referrals and asked to start sooner
options.feedback: Fewer clients, but they came on their own and were eager. That's pull, even if it doesn't look impressive yet.

options.text: Month 3: 40 clients filled in a survey saying they're satisfied
options.feedback: Nice to hear, and worth keeping. But saying you're happy costs nothing. Referrals and urgency show what people actually do.

cards.title: Fit is when customers pull, not when you push.
body: Product-market fit is a match between a product and a specific group who badly want it. You feel it when demand runs ahead of your effort.
**Try it today:** list where your last ten customers came from. How many found you on their own or through someone else, and how many did you have to chase?
